subject: Wong et al. (2017)
object: Wong et al. (2017) found that Nrros-deficient mice developed spontaneous neurological disorders, with motor defects and death before 6 months of age. Nrros-/- mice showed astrogliosis and lacked normal CD11b-hi/CD45-lo microglia, but had no detectable demyelination or neuronal loss. Instead, the CNS was populated by myeloid cells resembling perivascular macrophages.

subject: Wong et al. (2017)
object: Wong et al. (2017) deleted Nrros using a Cx3cr1-driven system and showed that it plays a crucial role in establishing microglia during early embryonic stages. They also found that NRROS, a transmembrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum expressed in myeloid cells, is required for normal expression of Sall1 and other microglial genes that are important for microglial development and function.

subject: Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) described 3 children from 2 families with a stereotyped phenotype: 2 sisters (P1 and P2) born to nonconsanguineous parents of Maori descent (family F1442), and a boy (P3) born to first-cousin South Asian parents (family F2382). Pregnancy, delivery and early development were normal. In the second year of life, the children developed refractory seizures and neurodegeneration, and they died between 27 and 36 months of age. Metabolic testing, including tests for mitochondrial dysfunction, did not find a cause.

subject: Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) reported that early neuroimaging in the 3 patients showed fine calcification at the depths of the cerebral gyri, with spot and linear calcification in the deep and subcortical white matter, and normal white matter signal. As the disease progressed, repeat imaging showed more calcification, rapidly progressive severe generalized cortical and subcortical atrophy with ventricular dilatation, and diffuse signal changes in the cerebral and cerebellar white matter.

subject: Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) reported that the postmortem examination of P3 found abnormalities only in the central nervous system. Findings included cerebral atrophy, focal calcification in the neuropil, and widespread neuronal loss with reactive gliosis. The most striking finding was an accumulation of foamy macrophages, mainly around blood vessels, throughout the cerebral and cerebellar white matter. These cells were positive for CD68, MHC class II and p22phox and negative for CD163, Iba1, NRROS, CD3, P2Y12 and TMEM119. Myelin basic protein was reduced, the U fibers were preserved, and there were occasional axonal spheroids. Parenchymal microglia were markedly abnormal, with loss of P2Y12 staining and weak TMEM119 staining.

subject: Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsense variant in NRROS, c.1777C>T (p.Gln593Ter), in the 2 affected sisters of Maori descent from family F1442. The variant is predicted to truncate the protein and had not been recorded before. No patient cells were available for functional studies.

subject: NRROS c.1777C>T / p.Q593*
Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous 1-bp deletion in NRROS, c.1257del (p.Gly420AlafsTer14), in a boy born to consanguineous South Asian parents (family F2382). The frameshift is predicted to truncate the protein and was present on only 1 of 251,438 alleles in gnomAD.

subject: NRROS c.1257del / p.G420A
Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) analyzed published transcriptomic datasets. In human brain, NRROS was expressed more than 50-fold higher in microglia than in whole brain, which the authors took to mean that microglia are the main cell type expressing NRROS in brain tissue. In mouse brain, Nrros was similarly enriched in microglia and was expressed even more highly in central nervous system perivascular macrophages.

subject: Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) reported marked upregulation of p22phox in perivascular macrophages in P3. They suggested that without functional NRROS, p22phox may bind NOX2 more, potentially increasing superoxide formation. They concluded that NRROS is essential for the early development and/or maintenance of a homeostatic microglial population, and that loss of NRROS function causes a new human microgliopathy. They noted no sign of immune-mediated inflammation.

subject: Smith et al. (2020)
object: Smith et al. (2020) noted that the patients' features resemble those of Nrros-deficient mice. These mice show progressive neurological decline starting at 2 to 3 months of age and die by 6 months. Their neuropathology includes neuronal loss, demyelination, axonal pathology, astrogliosis and foamy macrophages, all of which were seen in the patient examined. The mice also lose homeostatic microglial gene expression, including P2ry12 and Tmem119.

subject: Dong et al. (2020)
object: Dong et al. (2020) reported 6 individuals from 4 families with a neurodegenerative disease. All had refractory epilepsy, developmental regression, and reduced white matter volume with delayed myelination. Development was normal or mildly delayed at first. Seizures began within the first year of life and were followed by developmental regression. Intracranial calcification was detected in 3 of the individuals.

subject: Dong et al. (2020)
object: Dong et al. (2020) identified biallelic variants in the NRROS gene in 6 affected individuals from 4 families. The disease-causing variants affected 2 significant functional domains of NRROS. They produced aberrant proteins with an impaired ability to anchor latent TGF-beta-1 on the cell surface. The abstract does not name the individual variants.

subject: Dong et al. (2020)
object: Dong et al. (2020) expressed NRROS in HEK293T cells. Confocal microscopy showed that both wildtype and mutant NRROS colocalized with latent TGF-beta-1 inside the cell. Flow cytometry showed that the mutant proteins, unlike wildtype NRROS, failed to anchor latent TGF-beta-1 at the cell surface. Wildtype NRROS rescued this defect in the mutants.

subject: Dong et al. (2020)
object: Dong et al. (2020) concluded that loss of NRROS function causes a severe childhood-onset neurodegenerative condition. They suggested that its features point to a disordered response to inflammation. The patients' features were consistent with those of the Nrros knockout mouse and overlapped with the human condition associated with TGF-beta-1 deficiency.
